h1: Launching a gin brand in India without owning a distillery
title: Launch a Gin Brand Without a Distillery | Craft Beer School
desc: How to launch a gin brand in India without your own distillery: contract distilling, recipe ownership, licences, costs and risks.
teaser: You do not need your own still to start a gin brand. You do need a good partner, a clear agreement and a lot of working capital.
standfirst: Many craft gin brands begin without a still of their own. A contract distiller makes the gin to your recipe while you build the brand and sales. It is a faster start, but it comes with its own risks. Here is how to plan it.
sections:
In a brand-only model, a licensed distillery produces and bottles your gin. You own the brand, the recipe or at least the specification, the packaging and the route to market. The distillery owns the licences and the equipment. Breweries do the same with contract brewing, as our guide to contract brewing in India explains.

There are two broad versions. In one, you bring your own recipe, developed with a consultant or on a pilot still. The distillery makes it to your spec. In the other, the distillery offers a house gin, sometimes adjusted to your brief. The second is quicker but gives you less control and less to protect.

Spirits are regulated by each state in India. The distillery needs its manufacturing licence. As brand owner you will usually need label and brand registration in every state where the gin is sold. The gin must also move through each state's permitted supply chain, which in some states runs through a government corporation. Excise duty is generally paid in the state of sale. The rules, fees and timelines differ widely.

Work with a licensing consultant from the start. Getting a label approved in several states takes time. Launch plans often slip at this step.

Visit before you sign. Ask to see the still, the botanical store and the bottling line. Ask what other brands they make and how they keep recipes separate. Taste their existing products.

Ask for samples made to your recipe on their production still, not a lab still. Small and large stills give different results, so the gin you approve should come from the kit that will make it. Check that they can supply a consistent neutral spirit base, because that base is a large share of your gin's character.

• Recipe ownership and confidentiality. The recipe and specification belong to you and are not used for anyone else.
  • The specification. ABV with a tolerance, botanical list and weights, cut points if relevant, dilution water quality and a reference sample.
  • Botanical sourcing. Who buys them, to what grade and how substitutions are approved.
  • Batch approval. You or your representative taste and approve each batch against the reference before bottling.
  • Minimum runs and lead times. How much you must order and how far ahead.
  • Retained samples, complaints and recalls. Who keeps what and who pays when a batch fails.
  • Exit terms. How you move the recipe and your packaging stock if you leave.

Have a lawyer draft or review the agreement.
The money nobody warns you about

Gin is not cheap to launch even without a still. Bottles, closures, labels and cartons often have high minimum orders. Custom glass has long lead times. Excise duty may be due before the gin is sold. Distributors and retailers may pay on credit. Your cash is tied up for months between paying the distillery and getting paid by the market.

Build a cash flow forecast month by month, state by state, before you commit. Many brands run out of money on working capital rather than on production cost.

Without a distillery, your brand has to carry the story. Botanicals are the obvious hook: Indian citrus, spices and flowers give a gin a sense of place. Make sure the name and label are legally clear before you print anything. Our guide on naming a beer brand covers trademark checks that apply equally to gin.

Be honest about where the gin is made. Drinkers increasingly ask. A brand that hides its contract distiller can lose trust quickly when it comes out. Plenty of respected brands are open about it.
When to build your own still

Contract distilling suits the first years, when volumes are small and you are proving the brand. Over time, a brand that sells well may want its own still for control, margin and a visitor experience. That is a large step, with land, licences, equipment and staff. Wait until your sales history makes the case.

Either way, learn how gin is made. A founder who understands distillation asks better questions, spots problems in samples and earns the respect of the people making the product.
faqs: Can I sell gin in India without owning a distillery?
Yes. A licensed distillery can make and bottle your gin, but you will usually need your own brand and label registrations in each state of sale.
Who owns the recipe when a distillery makes my gin?
That depends on your agreement. Write in that the recipe and specification belong to you and stay confidential.
Why should samples come from the production still?
Small and large stills give different results. The gin you approve should be made on the kit that will produce it.
What is the biggest cost risk in launching a gin brand?
Working capital: packaging minimums, excise that may be paid before sale and slow payment from the market.
